header: Stereo. H C J D A 38.
Falak Sher Vs. Ch. Azhar Mehmood
J U D G M E N T
body: Date of Hearing: 17.11.2026 Appellant by: Sh. Usman Karim ud Din, Advocate.
On Court’s call: Mr. Imran Khan, Assistant Advocate General.
Respondent No.1: Proceeded against ex-parte vide order dated 10.11.2026.
Respondents No.2 and 3 by:
Mr. Awais Zafar, Advocate.

Anwaar Hussain, J. This appeal under Section 33 of the Punjab Consumer Protection Act, 2005 (“the Act”) is directed against the order dated 23.04.2024 passed by the Consumer Court, Gujranwala, whereby the appellant’s complaint was dismissed in limine, on the ground that he had purchased the fertilizer for a commercial purpose and, therefore, did not fall within the definition of the term “consumer”, under the Act.

2. The appellant is a private individual. Respondent No.1 is the proprietor of M/s. Warraich Brothers & Commission Agents, Galamandi, Gujranwala (“respondent-Commission Agent”). Respondents No.2 and 3 are the same company, arrayed through its Chief Executive Officer and General Manager, respectively (collectively referred to as “respondent- Fauji Fertilizer”). The appellant asserts that he purchased from the respondent-Commission Agent, the fertilizer represented to be a product of respondent-Fauji Fertilizer. He describes the fertilizer as faulty/counterfeited (جعلی) and claims that its use reduced the yield of his crop and, consequently, his profit.

3. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the Consumer Court invoked Section 2(c)(i) of the Act without giving effect to the Explanation thereof. The fertilizer, according to him, was purchased and used by the appellant in cultivating land to earn his livelihood, as a self-employed person. He relies upon case reported as Zaigham Imtiaz v. Iqbal Ahmed Ansari and another (2016 CLC 1145) in support of his contention wherein a complaint concerning a defective solar energy system installed and used at a shoe shop was entertained. He submits that the purpose for which the product was put to use was material in that case and ought likewise to have been examined here. Adds that, if disputed, the nature and purpose of the appellant’s cultivation required evidence for determination.

4. The respondents were proceeded against ex-parte on the last date of hearing i.e., 10.11.2026. Learned counsel for the respondent-Fauji Fertilizer has appeared today and seeks recall of that order. Learned counsel for the appellant has raised no objection. The order dated 10.11.2026 is accordingly recalled to the extent of the respondent-Fauji Fertilizer. The respondent-Commission Agent remains absent despite the fact that the name of his counsel is appearing in the cause list issued for today, and, hence, continues to be proceeded against ex-parte, in this appeal.

5. Learned counsel for respondent-Fauji Fertilizer also relies on the case of Zaigham Imtiaz supra. He draws attention of this Court to the observation in the said case that the object of a commercial undertaking is to earn profit. Referring to Paragraph 4 of the complaint, he submits that the alleged claim of decrease in profit, by the appellant, shows that the appellant purchased and used the fertilizer for a commercial purpose. He further submits that, if the fertilizer was counterfeit (جعلی), the appellant’s remedy lies under the law dealing with the counterfeiting. Learned counsel contends that Explanation to Section 2(c)(i) of the Act cannot undermine the plain meaning of the term ‘commercial purpose’.

6. Considering that the question concerns the rights of consumers throughout the Province, learned Law Officer was also heard on Court’s call. He submits that the Act is a beneficial legislation enacted for the protection of consumers’ rights and should receive a liberal construction that advances its object. Adds that the Explanation forms part of the statutory definition and must be given effect in determining the scope of “commercial purpose”, under Section 2(c)(i) of the Act.
7. Arguments heard. Record perused.
8. The following questions arise for determination:
(i) Whether an averment of diminished profit from reduced crop yield, by itself, warrants dismissal in limine of a complaint under section 2(c)(i) of the Act?
(ii) Whether the description of the fertilizer as counterfeit (جعلی) excludes the jurisdiction of the Consumer Court?

9. The preamble to the Act states its object in terms of protecting and promoting consumers’ rights and interests and providing speedy redress of their complaints. The Act defines the persons entitled to invoke that remedy and draws a distinction between commercial use, and use of the product for livelihood through self-employment. Expeditious disposal requires that the Court identifies the facts material to that distinction before deciding whether the complaint can proceed.
10. Section 2(c) of the Act, reads as follows.

“Consumer” means a person or entity who– (i) buys or obtains on lease any product for a consideration and includes any user of such product but does not include a person who obtains any product for resale or for any commercial purpose; or (ii) …….

Explanation.– For the purpose of sub-clause (i), “commercial purpose” does not include use by a consumer of products bought and used by him only for the purpose of his livelihood as a self-employed person.
(Emphasis supplied)

The two exclusions in Section 2(c)(i) of the Act concern the purpose for which the product in question was obtained. The product here is the fertilizer. On the appellant’s account, it was obtained for application to his crop. The produce raised with its use is a different commodity. Its sale, if any, does not constitute resale of the product—fertilizer. The question of commercial purpose remains, and has to be considered, subject to the Explanation.

11. The Explanation requires examination of both—the purpose of the purchase and the use of the product. A person who cultivates land through self-employment may earn his livelihood by selling what he grows. His receipts, after expenses, may constitute the income on which he depends. To hold that the possibility of such a return takes the purchase outside the Act would deprive the Explanation of effect in the very cases in which the self-employment generates income. Equally, an agricultural enterprise may purchase fertilizer for its commercial operations. The fact that the purchaser is an individual does not settle which of these situations applies. The nature and scale of the cultivation, the appellant’s own participation in it and the manner in which the operation was carried on may assist in determining whether the purchase and use were exclusively for the purpose specified in the Explanation. The statute prescribes no acreage or quantity of product as a test. Those matters may be relevant to the inquiry in a given case, but the finding must ultimately address the statutory purpose.

12. The submission that the Explanation, being explanatory in nature, cannot qualify the expression “commercial purpose” in Section 2(c)(i) of the Act is misconceived. An Explanation forms part of the enactment and must receive effect according to its language and purpose. Therefore, the Explanation must be read in conjunction with the substantive provision as its function is to clarify the meaning of that provision and assist its construction. Case reported as Muhammad Hussain Patel v. Habib Wali Muhammad (PLD 1981 SC 1), is referred wherein the Supreme Court held that an Explanation serves as a guide to the construction of the main provision. In case reported as S. Sundaram Pillai v. V.R. Pattabiraman [(1985) 1 SCC 591], the Supreme Court of India also held that an Explanation clarifies the meaning and operation of the provision to which it is attached. Here, the Explanation expressly prescribes the scope of “commercial purpose” by excluding products bought and used by the purchaser only for his livelihood as a self-employed person. The definition of “consumer” must, therefore, be applied with that qualification. Giving effect to the Explanation carries out the legislative intention expressed in the definition itself.

13. Adverting to the argument/emphasis on Paragraph 4 of the complaint that the purchase was for commercial purpose, and hence, complaint was not maintainable, it is imperative to reproduce the said para, which reads as under:

”ہیہکاسرطحےسہلمجخرہچہعمتمیقاھکد30,97,000/-رحبہہ فوسیتالھکاتسونےہراررفوےپاای ہکبجادمن ہلمج دیپافوار40,00,000/-رفوےپرحبفواچسیلالھک رفوےپ یھت اس رطح ےس انمعف 900,000/-وج اھت وتمعق رفوےپاوک اسلئ ےس فوہج یک رکےن ت فرفوخ اھکد یلعج وک اسلئ ےس رط یک پ 39,97,000/-رفوےپ ہرار)رحبفوااتنسیلالھکاتسونےرفوےپ ہرار)دیپافوار اییاصق وج وہا اصقنن اک یفوایلاھکد کیب ر ت وبہجیاصقاخراےئتDAPوسیاےکاامعتسلیکفوہجےسوہا“.

The said para speaks of diminished profit in explaining the consequence stated to have followed the use of the fertilizer. The assertion has to be read with the rest of the complaint. Even on the reading urged by learned counsel for the respondent-Fauji Fertilizer, it shows, at most, that the appellant expected a return from the crop and claims to have received less. The Consumer Court inferred from that averment that the purpose of buying and using the fertilizer was commercial, without examining whether the cultivation was the appellant’s means of earning a livelihood through self-employment. The use of the word “profit” in an averment in a consumer complaint about the loss cannot bear the weight placed upon it.

14. Reliance by both sides upon case of Zaigham Imtiaz supra needs to be examined as well. The judgment has been perused and considered. The complainant there carried on the business of selling shoes and had a solar energy system installed at his shop. When the system failed to work properly, he approached the Consumer Court. The seller challenged the interim order entertaining the complaint on the ground, inter alia, that the system had been used for a commercial purpose. This Court considered the purpose of the installation. It found that the system facilitated customers and workers and that there was no proof of its use for operating shoe-manufacturing machinery or supplying electricity to other shops. On those facts, it upheld the view that the complainant fell within Section 2(c)(i) of the Act. The interlocutory nature of the order was an additional ground for declining interference in the constitutional jurisdiction.

15. The reliance by the appellant side on case of Zaigham Imtiaz supra is well placed for the reason that the actual purpose of the transaction must be examined. The fact that both complaints concern allegedly defective products carries the analogy. The solar system was found to serve the convenience of the persons using the shop, whereas the fertilizer here was allegedly applied directly in raising the crop from which the appellant expected a return. This makes the purpose of the cultivation material. The appellant’s status must be determined by applying the Explanation to his own case.

16. The respondent-Fauji Fertilizer reads the observation concerning profit apart from the rest of the judgment in case of Zaigham Imtiaz supra. In said case, this Court considered the exclusion together with the Explanation to Section 2(c)(i) of the Act and, drawing upon case from the Indian jurisdiction that is reported as Laxmi Engineering Works v. P.S.G. Industrial Institute [(1995) 3 SCC 583] held that commercial purpose depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The observation in case of Zaigham Imtiaz supra, concerning the object of a commercial undertaking cannot convert every claim of diminished income/profit into an admission of commercial use. The case of Zaigham Imtiaz supra thus supports an inquiry into the purpose of the purchase. It supplies no basis for dispensing with that inquiry, in the present case, on the strength of Paragraph 4 of the complaint alone.

17. Corresponding jurisprudence on the subject from the neighboring jurisdiction also supports the case of the appellant. The judgment of the Supreme Court of India in case of M/s Nandan Biomatrix Ltd. v. S. Ambika Devi & Ors. (AIR 2020 SC 3136) is referred in this regard. Section 2(1)(d) of the Indian Consumer Protection Act, 1986, insofar as it excludes purchases for resale or commercial purpose and preserves purchases for livelihood through self-employment, is in pari materia with the provision under consideration. The Supreme Court of India, construing a provision in pari materia with Section 2(c)(i) of the Act and its Explanation, held that a small cultivator who bought planting material to raise a crop for her livelihood through self-employment was a consumer, even though the company had agreed to buy the produce at an assured profitable price. The same reasoning applies here. The appellant’s averment that his profit diminished because of reduced yield concerns the loss alleged and could not, by itself, justify dismissal in limine without examining whether he had bought and used the fertilizer solely to earn his livelihood through self-employed cultivation. The answer to the first question is that fertilizer is a “product” within the meaning of Section 2(j) of the Act, and its purchase and use by a cultivator exclusively to earn his livelihood through self-employment does not constitute a “commercial purpose” under Section 2(c)(i) read with its Explanation. Diminished profit has a nexus with the crop yield, which turned out to be less than expected yield. Suffice to observe that to an agriculturalist carrying out cultivation, as a self-employed person, less than the expected yield is, in itself, loss of profit. Therefore, an averment of diminished profit from reduced crop yield is, by itself, insufficient to hold that the fertilizer was purchased for a commercial purpose and to dismiss the complaint in limine.

18. As to the second question, the objection concerning counterfeiting was raised in this appeal by learned counsel for respondent-Fauji Fertilizer and was not the basis of impugned order. The complaint was dismissed in limine solely on the ground of commercial purpose. Whether the fertilizer described as جعلی was counterfeit or genuine but defective is yet to be examined by the Consumer Court. A finding on its nature or source at this stage would, therefore, be premature.

19. Moreover, this aspect bears on the respective liability of the respondents. If the fertilizer was counterfeit and sold as genuine, the respondent-Commission Agent’s liability would require examination along with any connection proved between respondent-Fauji Fertilizer and the goods, their supply or the representation under which they were sold. If it was a genuine but defective product, liability would fall to be determined under the provisions governing defective products. The dealership or distributorship, if any, and the source of the particular consignment are matters for evidence.

20. Even otherwise, Section 3 of the Act makes the remedies thereunder additional to those available under other laws. The answer to the second question is, therefore, that describing the fertilizer as جعلی—whether construed as counterfeit or defective, or the availability of proceedings concerning counterfeiting, does not by itself exclude a consumer claim otherwise maintainable under the Act. The Consumer Court shall determine the nature and source of the goods and the connection of each respondent with the transaction for deciding their respective liability in accordance with law.

21. In view of the above discussion, this appeal is allowed. The order dated 23.04.2024 is set aside. As a corollary, the complaint of the appellant shall be deemed to be pending before the Consumer Court, which shall afford the parties an opportunity of hearing and, where necessary, to lead evidence on maintainability under Section 2(c)(i) read with its Explanation of the Act and decide the matter afresh, in accordance with law.
(ANWAAR HUSSAIN)
JUDGE Approved for reporting.
